tasks.terminalSummary:
Section B's identities are all correct, and they hold for a wider family than stated. But nothing I found computes this binomial residue mod N without first exposing a factor some other way, so I reject it as a fast method. Verified improvement remains **NONE**.

The report is `research/findings/W022-binomial-separator-review.md`, with evidence in `W022-binomial-separator-review-evidence/`.

**Correctness: accepted, and the scope is wider**
- **Identities hold.** H_n(−1)=0 and H_n′(−1)=(−1)^m·n·C(2m,m), from (1−x²)^n and jC(n,j)=nC(n−1,j−1). n is a unit mod N, and the Lucas derivative argument holds as stated.
- **Simpler direct proof.** Applying Kummer/Lucas to C(2m,m) itself gives a stronger rule for every N≡3 (mod 4). Every prime factor ≡1 (mod 4) always divides it, because the lowest digit forces a carry. A prime factor ℓ≡3 (mod 4) divides it exactly when ℓ divides C((c−1)/2,(c−1)/4), where c=N/ℓ.
- **Scope repair.** Every semiprime N≡3 (mod 4) automatically has one factor in each residue class. So the stated family is all such semiprimes, not just close ones, and the gcd is always q or N. It equals q exactly when p∤C((q−1)/2,(q−1)/4). The condition q<2p is sufficient but not necessary: N=39, 203 and 979 all have q>2p and still give q. p=3 and unordered labels work.
- **N≡1 (mod 4).** Here the selector is undefined. The natural analog swaps the roles of the two residue classes: Blum moduli give N, and balanced pairs of primes ≡1 (mod 4) give 1. So this separates only semiprimes with one factor in each class; it is not an all-input splitter.

**Certificate: frozen before running, run once**
- All 26 cases matched the frozen predictions, using 11,335 of the 20,000 charged events.
- **Unbalanced cases:** these include four that give the full N: 87, 183, 791 and 19171.
- **Negative controls:** non-semiprime cases include N=231, all of whose primes are ≡3 (mod 4), which still gives 3.
- **Exact-arithmetic caveat:** the run used Python's exact `math.comb` with outputs up to 9,578 bits. The central coefficient has about N/2 bits, so the run means nothing about speed.

**Cost of getting the residue: no cheap method exists among known approaches; the shortcuts are circular**
- **Exact integer:** about N bits of work, which is worse than trial division.
- **Fraction-free form:** (2m)!/(m!)² is 0/0 mod N.
- **Ratio recurrence:** dividing by k+1 fails at k+1=min(p,q), so the run exposes the smaller factor itself.
- **Baby-step/giant-step methods for such recurrences (Chudnovsky; Bostan–Gaudry–Schost):** about √N ring operations, and they need inverses that fail at multiples of p or q. Finding the failing block is Strassen's factorial-gcd search: about N^{1/4}, or N^{1/5} with Harvey's algorithm. That search finds the smaller factor before the binomial value is ever reached.
- **Polylog extraction (Bostan–Christol–Dumas):** this only works in a known prime characteristic, which is the forbidden Lucas-in-unknown-p trick.
- **Equivalence:** an oracle for this gcd factors the family in one gcd step, and knowing the factors gives the gcd trivially. The separator is a re-encoding of the factor, not a mechanism. I make no hardness claim.

**Missing computation**
Given only N, compute C((N−3)/2,(N−3)/4) mod N, or any multiple of it coprime to p, below the factoring baseline. It must never invert a possible nonunit and must not use Frobenius at an unknown prime. I found no candidate.

**One different, paid route**
Use the group side of the same curve, y²=x³−x mod N, with an ECM-style ladder. It costs polylog operations per step. Because the curve has p+1 points mod p, this is exactly Williams' p+1 method, or Gordon's elliptic pseudoprime test when the multiplier is N+1. It is cheap but needs p+1 to be smooth. The binomial is deterministic but has no cheap extraction. A genuinely new route would need an object with both properties.

**Sources**
- **Exact match:** I found none in primary sources. I'm not claiming novelty.
- **Retrieved and read:**
  - [Bostan–Gaudry–Schost](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~eschost/publications/pollard.pdf)
  - [Costa–Harvey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.2116)
  - [Harvey, exponent one-fifth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05450)
  - [Bostan–Christol–Dumas](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.00545)
- **Downloads failed, recorded as citation only:**
  - [Shamir's 1977 MIT memo](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/148919)
  - Igusa 1958
  - Gordon 1989
- **Not attempted, cited from bibliographic records or abstracts only:** Kunihiro–Koyama 1998 and Chowla–Dwork–Evans 1986.
